items.abstract_text: With the widespread adoption of online educational technologies, instructional videos have become a pivotal tool for flexible and efficient learning. The integration of visual aids, such as animations and dynamic elements, aims to enhance the learning experience; however, their effectiveness remains debated. This study examined learning performance and subjective experience when instructional videos presented static AI-generated images or manually animated versions of those images. A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 40 undergraduate participants ( n = 10 per cell), comparing static versus motion-enhanced presentation conditions across male and female participant groups. Stable Diffusion XL generated the base images, and CapCut was used to add motion; the motion itself was not AI-generated. Participants viewed a 140-s mobile video on mortise-and-tenon structures, completed a 10-item accuracy test, and rated willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and mental effort. The ANOVA results provided no statistically significant evidence of a main effect of motion on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several subjective outcomes. For acceptability, the gender × motion interaction was statistically significant, but Bonferroni-adjusted simple-effect tests supported a gender-group difference only in the static condition. For mental effort, the interaction was also statistically significant; adjusted simple-effect tests indicated higher mental effort among female than male participants in the dynamic condition and higher mental effort in the static than dynamic condition among male participants. Given the small sample and multiple outcomes, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

Although average gender differences in spatial ability have been reported, they are small to moderate, highly variable across tasks and contexts, and often confounded with prior experience, technology familiarity, and confidence (Bartlett and Camba, 2023; Castro-Alonso et al., 2019) . For inclusive educational design, the goal is not to design "for males" or "for females," but to identify when motion helps or hinders different learners and to provide learner-controlled or adaptive options (Castro-Alonso et al., 2021) . This perspective motivates the present examination of whether responses to motion-enhanced AI-generated images differ across observed gender groups. This study employed a 2 × 2 between-subjects design, with two independent variables: "motion-enhanced AI-generated images" (static/dynamic) and "gender differences" (male/female). During the experimental design process, Illustrator software was used for graphic design, and CapCut was employed to produce the instructional videos. The experiment was conducted on an iPhone 11 device running iOS 15.7, featuring a 6.1 -inch Liquid Retina HD display. Participants watched an instructional video and subsequently completed a 10-item true/false test and a psychological evaluation questionnaire (collecting subjective data). Specifically, the dependent variables were learning accuracy, willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and perceived mental effort. Figure 1 shows the research framework of this study. Using purposive sampling, 40 undergraduate students (20 male; 20 female) were recruited via advertisement from a university in Shenzhen, China. A 2 (Gender: Male/Female) × 2 (Condition: Static/ Dynamic) between-subjects design was used. Forty participants were evenly distributed across the four experimental cells (Static-Male/ Static-Female/Dynamic-Male/Dynamic-Female), with n = 10 per cell. Stratified randomization was employed: participants were first stratified by gender, then randomly assigned to the static or dynamic video condition within each stratum. To control for prior knowledge, participants were explicitly screened to ensure they had no background in furniture design, woodworking, or architectural engineering, and specifically no prior knowledge of "mortise and tenon" structures. All participants possessed normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Before the experiment began, the researcher thoroughly explained the experimental purpose and safeguards. After fully understanding the relevant information, participants voluntarily signed a written informed consent form, confirming their rights to voluntary participation, informed consent, and withdrawal. Additionally, to avoid practice effects on the experimental results, all participants were first-time viewers of the experimental videos and were native Chinese speakers. All experimental protocols were approved by the Ethics Committee of Shenzhen Technology University under Approval No. SZTUYXLL2025113, a named institutional committee. Furthermore, written informed consent was obtained from all participants before participation. The experimental materials consisted of two versions of an online instructional video course on mortise-tenon structures. The visual assets were generated using a two-step workflow involving AI generation and manual editing to ensure both technical quality and pedagogical relevance. Negative prompts excluded distorted structures, artifacts, text, and cartoonish styles. analysis.discussion: Before discussing the implications of our findings, it is important to define the scope within which these results are most directly applicable. This study examined a specific type of instructional contentvisuospatially complex material (mortise and tenon structures) requiring understanding of three-dimensional relationships and assembly processes. The participants were higher education students with no prior domain knowledge, and the instructional videos were brief (140 s) and delivered on mobile devices. Therefore, our findings are most directly relevant to similar learning contexts: technical or procedural knowledge domains, novice learners, and short-format mobile learning environments. The present study investigated the effects of motion-enhanced AI-generated images in instructional videos on learning performance and subjective experience, with a particular focus on genderbased differences. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), this research aimed to elucidate whether dynamic visual presentations differentially impact male and female learners. The findings reveal a nuanced pattern: while motion effects alone did not significantly enhance learning accuracy, gender was associated with differences in objective performance and subjective evaluations. Significant interaction effects between gender and motion effects were observed for acceptability and mental effort, suggesting that responses to dynamic visual information may differ across gender groups; however, these differences should be interpreted cautiously because gender was not experimentally manipulated and relevant covariates were not measured. The present study yielded several noteworthy findings regarding the differential impact of motion-enhanced AI-generated images on male and female learners. A significant main effect of gender was observed, with male learners showing higher accuracy rates than female learners in this sample. However, this difference cannot be confidently attributed to spatial-processing ability, because the study did not measure baseline spatial ability, technology experience, general academic ability, or interest in the subject. Screening for prior woodworking knowledge does not ensure equivalence in these characteristics. Therefore, the accuracy difference may reflect unmeasured baseline differences, and this explanation should be treated as tentative. These findings address Q2 by indicating a difference between gender groups in this sample, but the underlying reasons remain unclear. This exploratory study examined learning performance and subjective responses to static versus motion-enhanced AI-generated images in a short mobile instructional video. No statistically significant evidence was found for a main effect of presentation condition on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several outcomes, but these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of inherent gender-based cognitive differences. For acceptability, a significant gender group × presentation condition interaction was observed. Bonferroni-adjusted simpleeffect tests indicated that female participants reported higher acceptability than male participants in the static condition, whereas the gender-group difference in the dynamic condition was not statistically significant. For perceived mental effort, the interaction was also significant: female participants reported higher mental effort than male participants in the dynamic condition, and male participants reported higher mental effort in the static than in the dynamic condition. The remaining adjusted comparisons were not statistically significant. These findings suggest that the effects of motion-enhanced visual presentation may vary across learners and outcomes rather than producing a uniform benefit. However, the small sample, absence of a formal manipulation check, limitations in measurement validation, multiple exploratory outcomes, and unmeasured learner characteristics constrain generalization. TAM-related perceptions and Cognitive Load Theory therefore serve as interpretive perspectives rather than as a tested integrated model. Future research should use larger samples, validated measures, appropriate analyses for bounded accuracy data, and learner-controlled or adaptive presentation based on measured needs and preferences rather than gender-based design prescriptions.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify the findings of this study and should be considered when interpreting the results. First, no formal manipulation check or independent image-quality assessment was conducted. We did not collect expert or participant ratings of visual quality, structural accuracy, semantic consistency, motion salience, or informational equivalence between the static and dynamic conditions. Although images were informally screened for visible artifacts and structural accuracy before inclusion, this screening served only as a material-selection step and does not constitute formal validation. We therefore cannot conclusively verify that participants perceived the static/dynamic distinction as intended, nor can we fully rule out artifact-related confounding. Future research should include manipulation checks and systematic ratings of visual quality, structural accuracy, semantic consistency, motion salience, and informational equivalence. Second, the measurement instruments have several limitations. No formal pilot testing was conducted. The reliability coefficients reported in the original manuscript were drawn from prior source studies rather than calculated in the present sample; sample-specific reliability estimates are now reported in Supplementary material but should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample size. The 10-item true/false accuracy test was reviewed for content validity by three experts, but no itemlevel analysis of difficulty, discrimination, or reliability was conducted. The acceptability scale was newly developed for this study and has not been formally validated; its factor structure, convergent validity, and discriminant validity remain unknown. The mental effort measure captures self-reported perceived effort and should not be interpreted as a pure measure of extraneous cognitive load. Future research should pilot-test all instruments, conduct item analyses, validate newly developed scales, and use measures that distinguish intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load more precisely. Third, the study does not test a full TAM model or provide measurement-model evaluation. TAM-related perceptions and Cognitive Load Theory are used as interpretive perspectives rather than as a tested integrated model. Willingness to continue learning is an intention-related evaluation, ease of understanding is perceived comprehensibility, preference is an affective evaluation of the video, and acceptability is a study-specific evaluation. No causal paths, factor structure, convergent validity, or discriminant validity are claimed. Future research should either validate adapted TAM constructs using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling or continue to use them as exploratory interpretive tools. Fourth, the sample size was small (N = 40; n = 10 per cell), and no a priori power analysis was conducted. Small or medium effects may therefore not have been detected. Nonsignificant results are reported as "no statistically significant evidence was found" rather than as proof that no difference exists, and 95% confidence intervals for nonsignificant effects are provided in Supplementary material. Future research should recruit larger and more diverse samples to detect small-tomedium effects. Fifth, several statistical issues require cautious interpretation. Learning accuracy was derived from 10 true/false items and is therefore bounded count data. A binomial generalized linear model would have been more appropriate than treating accuracy as a normally distributed continuous variable; however, the present study relied on ANOVA as an exploratory and comparability-oriented analysis, and no binomial GLM was conducted. In addition, because several dependent variables were examined, inflated Type I error cannot be ruled out; no formal multiplicity correction (e.g., Benjamini-Hochberg FDR) was applied, and interaction effects on secondary outcomes should therefore be interpreted as exploratory. Future research should use binomial or item-level mixed models for bounded accuracy data, report full assumption checks, apply appropriate multiplicity corrections, and provide effect sizes with confidence intervals. Accordingly, nonsignificant findings should be described as absence of statistically significant evidence rather than as evidence of no effect. Sixth, gender-related interpretations remain tentative. Gender was recorded as a binary category based on participant self-report; the source documentation does not specify whether this category reflects self-identified gender or biological sex, and no biological or essentialist interpretation is made. Gender was treated as an observed grouping variable, not as a causal or biological determinant. Baseline spatial ability, technology familiarity, general academic ability, anxiety, interest in woodworking, and prior experience were not objectively measured. Screening for prior woodworking knowledge does not ensure equivalence in these characteristics. The observed differences may therefore reflect unmeasured baseline differences, and they should not be used to prescribe different instructional treatments based solely on gender. Future research should include standardized measures of spatial ability, technology familiarity, and prior interest as covariates and should emphasize learner-controlled or adaptive presentation based on measured needs and preferences rather than gender-based design. Seventh, the qualitative component of this study is descriptive and lacks the methodological rigor expected of standalone qualitative research. The available record does not document participant selection beyond cell counts (three participants per cell, total N = 12; 6 male, 6 female), recording and transcription procedures, coding stages, number of coders, disagreement resolution, language and translation procedures, or criteria for thematic saturation. Interviews lasted 5-10 min and were conducted immediately after questionnaire completion. The interview comments are therefore presented as supplementary illustrations and should not be described as independently corroborating the quantitative findings. Future work should adopt established guidelines for rigorous thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006) , employ multiple independent coders with systematic reliability assessment, and provide comprehensive documentation of the analytic process. Eighth, the experimental materials and context limit generalizability. The dynamic condition used a mixed-process approach: base images were AI-generated using Stable Diffusion XL, but motion effects were manually applied using CapCut. This differs from pure AI-generated videos, which may exhibit different motion characteristics, temporal artifacts, or semantic inconsistencies. Exact generation and animation parameters are also incompletely documented, limiting reproducibility. items.abstract_text: Background and Aim: Evidence on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in secondary science education remains limited. This systematic review examined students’ conceptual understanding and engagement, teachers’ pedagogical strategies and challenges, and students’ critical thinking and scientific inquiry. Materials and Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, ERIC, Scopus, and Lens.org were searched for peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2022 and 2026. Two authors independently screened 187 unique records (Cohen’s κ = .78), identifying 20 eligible studies. Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Framework synthesis integrated findings, informed by Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK). Results: Seven studies assessed AI capabilities rather than classroom implementation. Only two compared learning outcomes across conditions; none employed a randomized controlled design. Student perceptions and engagement were generally positive, whereas learning outcomes were mixed. A chatbot supporting self-regulated learning outperformed a rule-based chatbot, but ChatGPT-4o yielded smaller gains than peer collaboration. Teachers reported concerns regarding content accuracy, assessment reliability, and instructional readiness. Generative AI matched or exceeded student performance on structured examinations but demonstrated lower grading reliability than human assessors. Evidence concerning critical thinking was particularly limited. Richer reasoning was reported with dialogue-oriented tools or teacher guidance, whereas answer-seeking use of general-purpose tools was associated with weaker reasoning. Conclusion: Pedagogical structuring was recurrently associated with productive AI use, although causal inference remains limited. A provisional model warrants empirical testing. Priorities include structured tasks, science-specific teacher development, human assessment oversight, explicit AI literacy instruction, school governance, and controlled comparisons of structured and unstructured use across secondary science classrooms.

items.abstract_text: As digital technology becomes more deeply embedded in education, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly present in junior high school students' daily learning. This paper explores the "scaffolding" role of GenAI in students' self-regulated learning (SRL) and its possible influence on enhancing academic self-efficacy. Based on Zimmerman's cyclical phase model of SRL and learning scaffolding theory, the study systematically deduces the human-AI interaction process. The analysis suggests that GenAI acts as planning, monitoring, and reflective feedback scaffolds across the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases, effectively addressing the lack of personalized support in traditional autonomous learning. Furthermore, GenAI assistance contributes to the internalization of academic self-efficacy by accumulating direct mastery experiences and alleviating trial-and-error anxiety. Acknowledging the potential risks of cognitive offloading and academic misconduct associated with GenAI dependency, the paper proposes coping strategies such as cultivating students' critical GenAI literacy and implementing dynamic scaffold fading. This research provides theoretical support and practical guidance for educators to optimize GenAI-assisted self-regulated learning environments.

items.title: Neural Mechanisms of Willed Attention Control

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Cueing paradigms are commonly used to study the neural mechanisms of visual spatial attention control. In these paradigms, each trial starts with an external cue, which instructs the subject to pay covert attention to a spatial location in anticipation of an impending stimulus (instructed attention). Recent work has introduced a new type of cue which prompts the subject to spontaneously decide which spatial location to attend (willed attention). We studied the neural mechanisms of willed attention control by analyzing fMRI and EEG data recorded at two institutions (UF and UC Davis) using the same willed attention paradigm. The findings include: (1) both instructional cues and the choice cue activated the DAN, (2) the choice cue additionally activated a frontoparietal decision network consisting of dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), anterior insula (AI), anterior prefrontal cortex (APFC), dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), and inferior parietal lobule (IPL), (3) the decision about where to attend can be decoded in frontoparietal decision network in choice trials but not in instructional trials, and (4) EEG alpha oscillation patterns immediately preceding the choice cue, but not the instructional cues, predicted the postcue direction of attention and the frontoparietal decision network activity. Based on these findings we proposed a model of willed attention control suggesting how the direction of visual spatial attention was decided upon in the absence of external instructions.

reading.interpretation: In this study, we analyzed fMRI and EEG data from two independent willed attention datasets, acquired using the same paradigm, to address the following questions. What is the neural network underlying willed attention control? What is the functional role of this willed attention control network? How does the neural activity prior to willed decisions about where to attend influence brain activations related to willed attention control? Participants discriminated the spatial frequency of the target grating appearing in the attended visual field as fast and accurately as possible through a button-press and ignored the grating appearing in the unattended visual field. The gratings were difficult to discriminate so that focused spatial attention was required for successful execution of the task. Compared to the probabilistic cueing used in the Posner style paradigms (Posner, 1980) , in which participants responded to the stimulus appearing in either visual field, the current design further encouraged the full deployment of focused covert spatial attention prior to the appearance of the stimulus. Following an inter-stimulus interval (ISI) randomized between 2000 and 8000 ms after the stimulus onset, participants were prompted by the visual cue "?SIDE?" to report the visual field they were attending on that trial through a button-press (self-report). This reporting was used to determine the direction of attention for willed attention trials but was included in instructed attention trials as well to maintain trial structure consistency. Reporting of the attended side was highly accurate across the participants with the accuracy of 98.4% averaged across conditions. For attention mappings which were randomized across participants. After a variable cue-to-target interval (2,000-8,000 ms), a target stimulus (a grating with high or low spatial frequency) appeared briefly (100 ms) with equal probability in either visual field. Participants were asked to discriminate the spatial frequency of the grating presented at the cued or chosen location (attended location), while ignoring stimuli on the uncued or unchosen side (unattended location). Following a variable interstimulus interval (ISI; 2,000-8,000 ms), a "?SIDE?" prompt appeared, asking participants to report the visual field they attended to on that trial. Finally, a variable inter-trial interval (ITI; 2,000-8,000 ms) elapsed before the onset of the next trial. Neuroscience instructed attention trials, side reporting accuracy could be determined by comparing the selfreport with the cue instruction, while for willed attention trials, the accuracy was determined by examining the consistency between the participant's response (or lack of response) and the selfreport. An inter-trial interval (ITI) randomized between 2000 and 8000 ms was inserted after the self-report. This ITI is critical for generating uncertainty about when the next cue would occur, thus making it impossible for the subject to choose where to attend in advance of the choice cue within a narrow time window. Prior to recording, all participants went through a training session to familiarize with the task and to ensure stable performance (above 70% accuracy). During recording, the experiment was divided into blocks of trials with the length of each block kept around six minutes. All participants completed at least eight blocks of trials. For willed attention, participants were explicitly told to avoid relying on any stereotypical strategies of generating decisions, such as always attending the same/opposite side they attended during the previous trial, as well as to avoid randomizing or equalizing their decisions to choose left or right across trials; prior studies found that decisions to explicitly randomize decisions might invoke additional working memory related processes (Spence & Frith, 1999 ) . UF fMRI: fMRI data were acquired using a 3T Philips Achieva scanner (Philips Medical Systems, Netherlands) with a 32-channel head coil. Functional images were obtained using a single-shot echo planar imaging (EPI) sequence with the following parameters: repetition time (TR) = 1980 ms, echo time (TE) = 30 ms, flip angle = 80°, field of view = 224 mm. Thirty-six transverse slices (slice thickness: 3.5 mm) oriented parallel to the plane connecting the anterior and posterior commissures were obtained in an ascending order with a voxel resolution of 3.5×3.5×3.5 mm 3 . UF EEG: Continuous EEG data was recorded inside the MRI scanner simultaneously with fMRI using a 32-channel MR-compatible EEG recording system (Brain Products, Germany). Thirty-one Ag/AgCl electrodes were located on the scalp according to the 10-20 system via an elastic cap. One additional electrode was located on the participant's upper back to record the electrocardiogram (ECG), which was used to remove the ballistocaridogram (BCG) artifacts (Ertl et al. 2010) . The FCz channel was used as a reference during recording. The impedance of all scalp channels was kept under 5 kΩ throughout the experiment. The sampling frequency was 5000 Hz. UCD fMRI: fMRI data were acquired using a 3T Siemens Skyra scanner (Siemens, Germany) with a 32-channel head coil. Functional images were obtained using a single-shot EPI sequence with the following parameters: TR = 2100 ms, TE = 30 ms, flip angle = 90o, field of view = 218 mm, slice thickness = 3.4 mm. Thirty-four transverse slices were obtained in an interleaved acquisition order. The voxel resolution was 3.5×3.5×3.5 mm 3 .

items.abstract_text: Against the backdrop of generative AI emerging as a core strategic asset for major powers, the rhetorical tropes of national security and industrial competitiveness are subject to strategic manipulation by divergent domestic actors. The deregulatory camp within the White House invokes industrial competitiveness to roll back security-focused executive orders; the security faction in Congress expands chip export controls in the name of national defense; state-level authorities counter federal overreach through consumer protection mandates; and Silicon Valley deploys a two-pronged lobbying strategy. Taking the 2023-2026 policy pendulum and BIS chip regulations as its analytical case, this paper demonstrates that domestic contestation spills over globally through transmission channels. This has produced a global AI governance landscape defined by fragmentation, hollowed-out soft law processes, and a three-bloc divide across the U.S., the EU, and China, while the shortening commitment half-life of U.S. policy positions has inflated the costs of multilateral cooperation. The study also identifies limited positive spillover effects. In response, the paper puts forward targeted strategies. The conclusion argues that U.S. internal regulatory divisions constitute a mechanism that externalizes domestic political costs as global governance uncertainty. Understanding this mechanism is a prerequisite for reshaping the multilateral AI order.

items.abstract_text: With AI agents increasingly involved in teamwork, whether AI can substitute human collaboration has become a heated topic in academia. Large-model-driven agents are now capable of participating in team brainstorming, task coordination, and collaborative problem-solving, and knowledge-intensive industries are beginning to form a large number of human-machine hybrid teams. Existing research mostly relies on theoretical reasoning and lacks empirical perceptual data from front-line practitioners. Drawing on a questionnaire survey of 158 employees with cross-industry teamwork experience, this paper explores practitioners' perceptions regarding the substitution of human collaborative behaviors by AI. The results show that AI can only partially substitute procedural and rule-oriented collaborative tasks, whereas social-emotional communication, conflict mediation and value judgment remain irreplaceable human strengths. Position, work experience and AI familiarity jointly shape individual perceptions of the substitution boundary. Most practitioners regard AI as an auxiliary tool rather than a leader of team collaboration. This study provides a practical reference for enterprises applying AI collaboration tools.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Digital transformation is reshaping academic work through remote and hybrid arrangements, intensified digital connectivity and the expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI). These developments can support flexibility, autonomy and efficiency, but may also intensify workload, erode work–life boundaries and generate demands associated with continuous adaptation, academic integrity and professional responsibility. Existing evidence is fragmented across technostress, remote and hybrid work, digital readiness and AI-enabled academic work, leaving insufficiently explained how technological change becomes embedded in the organisation and experience of academic work and, through this process, relates to wellbeing. This conceptual paper addresses this gap by developing the Digital Academic Work Reconfiguration and Wellbeing (DAWR-W) Framework. The framework was developed through theory synthesis informed by a structured literature foundation of 40 empirical studies and complementary theoretical research. The synthesis distinguishes the characteristics through which digital transformation reconfigures the organisation, boundaries, demands, relationships and professional content of academic work from the psychosocial mechanisms through which academics experience these changes. The resulting framework identifies seven characteristics of digitally transformed academic work and six psychosocial mechanisms involving resource depletion and replenishment, recovery and psychological detachment, perceived control and autonomy, competence and adaptive capacity, relational connection and psychological safety, and professional meaning and identity. Organisational and institutional conditions shape how digital transformation becomes embedded in academic work, while boundary conditions and feedback processes recognise contextual variation and adaptation over time. The central contribution of the DAWR-W Framework is to position work reconfiguration, rather than technology exposure alone, as the occupational process connecting digital transformation with academic employee wellbeing. In doing so, the framework integrates previously fragmented digital-work phenomena within a common explanatory architecture and locates responsibility for sustainable digital academic work across both individual and institutional levels. It provides an occupation-specific foundation for empirical testing, work-design interventions, and digital and AI governance in higher education.

items.abstract_text: This study investigates the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) among first-year English majors at Hanoi Open University. Using a mixed-methods approach, the research explores how Generative AI tools—such as ChatGPT and Bing Chat—serve as pedagogical "launchpads" rather than intellectual "crutches". Key findings show that AI feedback significantly strengthens the SRL cycle by helping learners decompose goals and providing immediate, non-judgmental diagnostic support. Notably, learners demonstrate high levels of "Technological Self-efficacy" and actively cross-verify AI outputs to mitigate the risk of "hallucinations." The study concludes that AI promotes independent thinking and adaptive help-seeking when positioned as a "debating partner." These results offer vital insights for higher education transitions, suggesting that AI-integrated frameworks can optimize self-learning capacity and cultivate the critical evaluation skills necessary for the Education 4.0 era.

items.venue: Assoeltan Indonesian Journal of Community Research and Engagement

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping science education by expanding access to information, supporting adaptive instruction, enabling simulations, and providing timely feedback. This article examines the opportunities, challenges, and implications of AI integration for students’ critical thinking in the digital era. Using a narrative literature review, the study synthesizes foundational scholarship on AI in education, science learning, AI literacy, and critical thinking, alongside recent reviews and international guidance. The synthesis indicates that AI can support critical thinking when it is embedded in inquiry-oriented activities that require students to formulate questions, interpret scientific evidence, compare explanations, identify limitations, and justify conclusions. AI-supported simulations, conversational systems, and feedback tools may make abstract concepts more accessible and provide opportunities for iterative reasoning. However, these benefits are not automatic. Hallucinated information, algorithmic bias, privacy risks, unequal access, academic integrity concerns, and cognitive over-reliance may weaken learning if AI outputs are accepted without verification. The article argues that AI should function as a cognitive partner rather than a substitute for students’ intellectual work. Effective integration therefore requires scientific and AI literacy, teacher mediation, transparent assessment, ethical safeguards, and learning tasks that make reasoning visible. A human-centred approach can help science education use AI to strengthen, rather than displace, independent and evidence-based thinking.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how knowledge workers make sense of GenAI-enabled co-production, with particular attention to authorship ambiguity and its implications for competence attribution, self-evaluation and meaningful work. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a qualitative approach based on in-depth interviews with 32 knowledge workers who work directly with GenAI tools, combining inductive coding with abductive interpretation. We used the Gioia methodology to analyze participants' reported experiences and interpretations of human–AI collaboration, with sensemaking informing the interpretation of emergent themes and aggregate dimensions. Findings The findings identify authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. When GenAI contributes to ideation, analysis, drafting, coding or other knowledge-intensive outputs, workers may find it difficult to distinguish their own contribution from that of the technology. Participants responded to this ambiguity differently. Some reconstructed their expertise around judgment, validation and contextualization and experienced GenAI as extending their professional capability. Others struggled to internalize successful outputs as evidence of their own competence and reported impostor-like experiences and reduced meaningfulness. The findings suggest that experiences of GenAI-enabled co-production depend on whether workers interpret and reconstruct their contribution. Practical implications Managers in comparable knowledge-intensive settings may consider making human judgment visible, clarifying legitimate uses of GenAI and recognizing contributions beyond output speed and quality. Originality/value This study identifies authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. It shows how uncertainty regarding the respective contributions of the worker and GenAI can complicate competence attribution and initiate sensemaking about professional contribution. By explaining how workers' interpretations of authorship ambiguity are associated with divergent identity and meaning outcomes, including enhanced capability, impostor-like experiences and changing meaningfulness, the study extends research on human–AI collaboration beyond its predominant focus on performance and productivity.

Across a rigorous crossgenerator generalization protocol, HexMIL outperforms all baselines by +9.1 AUC and +9.4 F1 in classification and achieves the best average IoU and PG in localization without any spatial supervision. items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Natural language processing and AI models are increasingly used to extract emotional signals from textual data; however, systematic validation of different computational paradigms in emotionally complex relational contexts remains limited. Such approaches may contribute to digital health research, particularly in the fields of digital mental health and couples therapy, where understanding emotional expressions within romantic relationships is especially relevant. Objective This study aimed to compare a lexicon-based approach (NRC Emotion Lexicon) and a transformer-based model (Pysentimiento) in detecting affective patterns within spontaneous romantic relationship narratives and to evaluate their criterion-related associations with a theory-driven measure of relational well-being. Methods In this cross-sectional exploratory study, 112 Spanish adults completed the Couple Flourishing Measure (CFM) and provided an open-ended description of their romantic relationship. Narratives were analyzed using both computational approaches to generate emotion and sentiment indices. Pearson correlations were computed between model outputs and CFM scores. Steiger Z tests were conducted to compare dependent correlations across models. Results Both approaches showed significant associations with couple flourishing, although the transformer-based model yielded stronger correlations for several affective dimensions, particularly positive sentiment ( r =0.66, 95% CI 0.54-0.76) and negative sentiment ( r =−0.74, 95% CI −0.82 to −0.65). The lexicon-based approach showed smaller associations, primarily for negative emotions. Steiger Z tests identified significant between-model differences for disgust ( P =.04), joy ( P =.01), sadness ( P =.004), surprise ( P =.03), and positive and negative sentiment (both P <.001), but not for anger or fear. Conclusions In this sample, Pysentimiento showed stronger associations with couple flourishing than the NRC Emotion Lexicon across several affective dimensions, although differences were not consistent across all categories. These findings support the value of theory-driven external criteria for evaluating computational emotion detection in relational narratives and underscore the importance of context-sensitive interpretation when applying AI tools in psychologically sensitive domains. These findings also highlight the potential relevance of computational emotion analysis for digital health research, particularly in digital mental health and couples therapy research, although further validation in clinical settings is needed before clinical implementation.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background AI is increasingly embedded in health care and digital health applications, shaping clinical processes as well as how patients access information and participate in care. Research on bias in medical AI has largely focused on technical and performance-related disparities. Less attention has been paid to how such biases may affect patients’ access, understanding, trust, and opportunities for meaningful involvement in care. Objective This scoping review aimed to map how studies of bias in medical AI describe patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment and the digital divide and to identify gaps across technical, social, structural, and patient-centered perspectives. Methods This scoping review followed JBI (Joanna Briggs Institute) methodology and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) reporting guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE and EBSCOHost databases were searched in August 2025 and supplemented by Google Scholar searches. Peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 onward were included if they addressed bias in medical AI and described patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment or digital inequality. Data charting focused on AI application types, bias dimensions, patient empowerment domains, digital divide–related factors, intersectionality, and debiasing strategies. Findings were synthesized descriptively and thematically. Results The search identified 497 records, of which 22 studies met the inclusion criteria. Bias was represented as a multidimensional sociotechnical phenomenon, with social bias identified most frequently (21/22 studies), followed by algorithmic bias (16/22 studies), structural bias (14/22 studies), and design-related bias (12/22 studies). Patient empowerment was most frequently addressed through involvement in care (n=13), followed by health literacy (n=9) and trust and assurance (n=7), whereas broader psychosocial and everyday-life domains were addressed less frequently. Digital divide–related factors were identified in 19 of the 22 studies, with digital literacy and usability barriers reported most frequently. Seven studies considered 2 or more social or structural dimensions of disadvantage. Although many studies discussed approaches that could mitigate bias-related barriers, explicit empirical evaluation of debiasing strategies in relation to patient empowerment or digital equity was largely absent. Conclusions Patient-related consequences of bias in medical AI extend beyond algorithmic performance and are reflected in access, understanding, trust, and involvement in care. Broader empowerment dimensions, multidimensional disadvantage, and empirically evaluated mitigation strategies remain comparatively underexplored.

items.abstract_text: Introduction Watershed environmental governance increasingly combines dense sensing infrastructure with institutions whose attention, authority, and coordination capacity remain limited. We develop the cognitive orchestration layer as a theory-building concept for examining how large language model (LLM)-based agents may connect sensing, assessment, decision advice, institutional response, and feedback without displacing domain models or public authority. Methods The Agentic Framework for Watershed Governance (AFWG) specifies three enabling pathways, three institutional interfaces, and four propositions. A purposively selected set of eight publicly documented cases is used to illustrate functional configurations, source limitations, and research gaps; it is not a systematic review or empirical evaluation. Results The cases document sensing, assessment, and decision-support functions, but do not establish improved decision quality, sustained institutional use, environmental outcomes, or agent-executed response closure. MAESTRO is retained as an adjacent-domain design illustration, not an existence proof of full-loop closure: human authorization remains necessary, and its reported performance has not been independently replicated. Discussion Transfer to watershed governance is plausible only where domain models remain authoritative, outputs carry provenance and uncertainty, named officials retain authority to authorize consequential actions, and institutional audit and failure handling are built into deployment. AFWG therefore offers a bounded conceptual framework and a falsifiable research agenda, rather than a claim that agents have already closed the watershed response loop.

These measures reduce particular assessment biases within the authors' study; they do not establish replication by an external research team or a causal reduction in disaster losses. Accordingly, we use these results only to characterize the reported technical evaluation, not to validate AFWG or infer watershed effectiveness. The sources describe different deployment stages rather than necessarily conflicting dates. Wang et al. (2026) report integration or operation from mid-2024, whereas an official Zhejiang account records a formal launch on 16 April 2026 and use for that flood season (Zhejiang Provincial Department of Emergency Management, 2026). A later formal announcement does not, by itself, confirm or disprove earlier operation. We therefore distinguish the publicly announced launch from the paperreported earlier use, which lacks independent corroboration in the inspected material. Neither date supplies an independently validated operational benchmark. Under the manuscript's definitions, MAESTRO does not close the agent-executed response ring. Its outputs are recommendations, and human authorities retain the power to issue warnings and mobilize action. The case may illustrate how an agent participates in a broader socio-technical loop that institutions can close, but it cannot simultaneously be coded as autonomous full-loop closure. In Table 6 , sensing, assessment, and decision advice are sourcereported; feedback and audit features are architectural provisions; response remains human-authorized. The cited study acknowledges limitations including the absence of prospectively defined impact indicators and a counterfactual design, restricted application domains, an incomplete cost-benefit analysis, the time required for integration, and a focus on early warning (Wang et al., 2026) . The present analysis also distinguishes internal evaluation safeguards from external validation and early operation from formal launch. MARSHA/WildfireGPT is a peer-reviewed consultative hazardadaptation prototype (Xie et al., 2025) . In its 2025 report, the OECD described FEMA's Planning Assistant for Resilient Communities (PARC) as a generative-AI initiative intended to assist governments with hazard-mitigation planning and the preparation of draft plan elements (OECD, 2025, Box 5.58) . First, procure orchestration through a staged gateway: sandbox evaluation, supervised pilot, limited operational release, and independent review before scale-up. Second, assign every recommendation a named receiving official, legal authority, deadline, escalation path, and override field; no consequential work order should be issued without an auditable authorization record. Third, require a model-and-data register listing approved domain models, rule versions, retrieval corpora, tool permissions, update dates, and documented uncertainty ranges. Fourth, create a minimum feedback schema linking alert, recommendation, authorization, action, implementation status, field observation, override, incident, and outcome identifiers across agencies. Fifth, establish an independent audit function with log access, red-team testing, supplier separation, anomaly review, and authority to suspend the system. Sixth, publish a standard evaluation dashboard covering assessment latency, citation completeness, error and abstention rates, human review time, override rates, authorized response time, feedback completeness, and environmental outcomes. These measures translate interface-based deployment, open evaluation data, and parallel auditing into procurement and operating requirements rather than general appeals.

AiNS's officedrafting and compliance-review functions are excluded from the loop mapping; its reported digital-twin and prediction functions are mapped only where the source provides operational detail. The Shangshan framework is treated as a reported technical framework rather than an officially validated deployment because the accessible report identifies commercial source material and disclaims endorsement. These decisions are visible in the supplementary matrix. Case mapping remains an interpretive, single-team exercise. Checking the matrix against its stated rules is not independent human double coding, and no inter-coder agreement statistic is reported. In particular, internal consistency cannot establish the reliability of judgments at the assessment-decision and decisionresponse boundaries. The published rules, provenance fields, and separate interpretation columns make those judgments inspectable without presenting an internal check as independent validation. Figure 3 is a case-by-ring matrix for the included set only; it does not depict density or prevalence, or establish the absence of cases outside the bounded scan. This paper has six limitations. First, it does not estimate causal effects. Second, the original eight cases are purposive illustrations without a population frame or a complete historical screening log; the supplementary searches extend the evidence considered but do not create a population frame. Third, many deployment claims are source-reported and lack independent outcome evaluation. Fourth, MAESTRO is adjacent-domain evidence, and the separate accounts of early operation and formal launch do not establish independently validated performance. Fifth, the interpretive mapping has not undergone independent human double coding. Sixth, the institutional adaptations developed here are design arguments, not validated cross-national findings. The Chinese observations establish particular integration and warning-response problems, not their national prevalence or the effectiveness of an agentbased remedy. The revision strengthens transparency through documented source-verification and topic-based searches, record-level exclusions, explicit appraisal of additional studies, claim-level mapping, and metric-specific provenance. Test P3. Conduct process tracing of cross-boundary waterpollution or flood events, contrasting how knowledge orchestration affects coordination costs under different dataownership arrangements. Compare indicator behavior and data quality between deployments with and without institutionalized auditing, observing whether strategic responses emerge and whether auditing suppresses them. Test institutional adaptation. The adaptations developed in the preceding discussion provide specifications to evaluate, rather than leaving institutional transfer undefined. Compare whether recipient-and-authority mapping, joint authorization, and participatory feedback function as intended within comparable workflows. MAESTRO, PARC, and MARSHA/WildfireGPT should not be ranked by raw speed or agreement figures because their tasks, institutional roles, and evaluation designs differ. Comparative studies should instead examine matched mechanisms such as lawful routing, handling of disagreement, authorized action, and review of outcomes.

items.abstract_text: The study aimed to check the association of ChatGPT use and critical thinking on academic integrity. The research design is cross-sectional correlational study to collect data from university students aged from 18 to 23 years old. The sample size was 600 students taken via purposive sampling from the University of Gujrat, Pakistan. Standardized psychological scales of ChatGPT usage scale, critical thinking evaluation scale, and academic integrity scales were used. Our findings showed that ChatGPT has no significant effect on academic integrity but has positive effect on critical thinking. While critical thinking has positive effect on academic integrity. It showed that ChatGPT doesn’t directly change cheating behavior, but it can boost critical thinking for students, and that improved critical thinking is what increases academic integrity. Implications of the findings are discussed.

analysis.discussion: The study aimed to explore the relationship between ChatGPT use, critical thinking skills and academic integrity among university students. The present research aimed to check whether the ChatGPT and critical thinking skills both positively influence on the academic integrity among students, or ChatGPT have no influence on academic integrity or the critical thinking skills have positively influenced on academic integrity. H1 stated that there is significant relationship between ChatGPT use, critical thinking, and academic integrity among university students: The first hypothesis was supported as the results indicate a significant positive correlation between ChatGPT and critical thinking skills, indicating that students use ChatGPT information by using their critical thinking skills by evaluating and analyzing the information. The students at university show positive relations that mean they not just use ChatGPT to do assignments and academic tasks but also use it for enhancing their critical thinking skills in their academic tasks. The present results are consistent with the study by (Suriano et al., 2025) , that investigates how students interact with AI chatbots like ChatGPT and the factors like attitude, trust, engagement, and knowledge about AI plays the role. The researchers found students' trust in AI. Eventually, engagement with AI influences critical thinking skills than simple knowledge of AI. The study suggests that AI chatbots can focus on the development of critical thinking skills but only when students are actively engaged and analyze information carefully rather than accept it without reflecting it. The study relates in a way that proper use of ChatGPT may increase the critical thinking skills in students. The present results are consistent with previous studies (Nugroho &Trisusana, 2024; Syahsaputra, & Ni'matuzahroh, 2026) whose findings showed that many students use AI for writing assignments, understanding topics, summarizing information and generating ideas. Students believe that using AI for writing and help is acceptable but using it for completing assignments was disheartening and dishonesty. Therefore, they used their metacognitions to evaluate positive use of the AI tools. Another study examined how ChatGPT impacts secondary students' critical thinking skills by using survey-based quantitative approach. The data were collected from 300 students. The results show that most students believe that AI tools like ChatGPT improve their critical thinking skills as compared to those who haven't used it or used it often less. The research also found a positive relationship between ChatGPT use and critical thinking skills (Zafar et al., 2025) . H2 stated that critical thinking mediates the association between ChatGPT use and academic integrity.The results in figure 1 indicate that ChatGPT usage was not significantly associated with academic integrity (beta = .07, p = .15), whereas critical thinking significantly and fully mediated the relationship between ChatGPT usage and academic integrity (beta = .23, p < .001). Previous research suggests that students commonly use ChatGPT for brainstorming, paraphrasing, writing assistance, and information retrieval, but concerns remain regarding plagiarism, overreliance, and inaccurate references. Ethical and responsible use including transparency, source verification, proper citation, and plagiarism avoidance facilitate students to protect academic integrity (Kanashina, 2026; Shishakly, 2025) . ChatGPT needs to be treated as a supportive learning tool in critical thinking rather than a replacement for students' own reasoning and academic work (Sallam, et al., 2024; Susnjak, 2023; Tlili, et al., 2023) . The systematic review of literature showed how integrating AI technologies like ChatGPT can change practices of assessments. AI tools support learning, but at the same time they also challenge academic integrity, originality, and exploring students' original abilities. Traditional assessments approaches like essay writing are more vulnerable for generative AI misuse, which may push educators to think again about how students are being evaluated. The research also demonstrates using AI resistant methods like oral exams and multi-stage assessments is the better way to understand and measure critical thinking. It also explains the institutional policies and digital literacy practices to encourage the proper use of technology (Ncube et al., 2025) . The first limitation is that this study used self-report questionnaire and the second is the sample size. The sample size was small so can't generalize results this on the population and the self-report questionnaire might introduce biasness. The first strength of this research is that it added to existing literature and studied the interrelation between ChatGPT, academic integrity and critical thinking. The second strength of this study is that it only conducted in Western context, this study never happened before in Pakistan context. Future researchers will use longitudinal study design to see the impact of these variables over time. Future research will expand the sample size and replicate the study across multiple universities to improve generalizability of findings.In conclusion, this study provides evidence that ChatGPT, critical thinking and academic integrity among university students are strongly correlated with each other. The path analysis in structure equation model confirmed that ChatGPT is not directly influence on academic integrity but critical thinking has significantly positively mediated with ChatGPT and academic integrity.
